research_text:
## Research brief

### 1. Governed API and the event/value to which this finding refers

`java.security.spec.ECGenParameterSpec` is an immutable `AlgorithmParameterSpec` used to specify EC domain parameters for parameter generation by a **standard or predefined name**. Its sole constructor is:

```java
ECGenParameterSpec(String stdName)
```

The JDK API describes `stdName` as “the standard name of the to-be-generated EC domain parameters,” directs users to the Java Security Standard Algorithm Names specification, and says supported names must be confirmed in the documentation for the provider that will implement the operation. The constructor documents `NullPointerException` for a null name; it does not document validation or cryptographic use at construction time.  
Direct source: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/spec/ECGenParameterSpec.html ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/spec/ECGenParameterSpec.html))

For the reported rule specifically, the finding refers to the **single `stdName` argument at construction** of `ECGenParameterSpec`, not to:

- a `KeyPairGenerator`, `AlgorithmParameterGenerator`, `Signature`, or `KeyAgreement` call;
- a provider lookup or a provider’s eventual acceptance of the name;
- generated keys, encoded keys, or a protocol/wire-format field.

The rule’s `SPEC` target is `java.security.spec.ECGenParameterSpec`; its sole event is the one-argument constructor event `ECGenParameterSpec(stdName)`. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/ECGenParameterSpec.crysl))

### 2. Documented correct/safe usage and documented remediation

#### Documented usage

The official JDK documentation supports the following limited conclusions:

1. Construct the parameter spec with a **non-null standard or predefined EC-parameter name**. The API directs consumers to the Java Security Standard Algorithm Names specification and to the selected provider’s documentation for supported names.  
   Direct sources:  
   https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/spec/ECGenParameterSpec.html  
   https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/specs/security/standard-names.html ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/spec/ECGenParameterSpec.html))

2. The Java SE 25 standard-names document expressly says that `ECGenParameterSpec` “may be used to specify a set of elliptic curve parameters” using its listed names. Its current list includes, among others, `secp224r1`, `secp256k1`, `secp256r1`, `secp384r1`, `secp521r1`, selected binary-field `sect*` curves, and `brainpoolP256r1`, `brainpoolP384r1`, and `brainpoolP512r1`. Thus, the Java SE 25 standard-name list is not the same finite set as the detector rule’s constraint list.  
   Direct source: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/specs/security/standard-names.html ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/specs/security/standard-names.html))

3. Java Security Standard Algorithm Names are documented as **not case-sensitive**. An analysis rule that only enumerates lowercase spellings therefore does not itself establish that differently cased standard-name input is invalid under the Java standard-names specification.  
   Direct source: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/specs/security/standard-names.html ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/specs/security/standard-names.html))

4. A parameter spec can be supplied to an algorithm-specific `KeyPairGenerator.initialize(AlgorithmParameterSpec)` call. The JDK documents that the provider may reject inappropriate parameters with `InvalidAlgorithmParameterException`; it also documents that provider-specific defaults are used if a key-pair generator is not explicitly initialized.  
   Direct source: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyPairGenerator.html ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyPairGenerator.html))

#### Provider-specific guidance

The standard-names document allows an SE implementation to support algorithms beyond the Java SE list and says implementations should document such support. Consequently, standard-name status alone does **not** establish that a particular provider or deployment supports a name.  
Direct source: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/specs/security/standard-names.html ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/specs/security/standard-names.html))

For the **JDK 25 SunEC provider specifically**, Oracle documents `secp256r1`, `secp384r1`, and `secp521r1` as “Recommended Curves,” and identifies their OID and aliases. It states, for example, that `secp256r1`, `1.2.840.10045.3.1.7`, `NIST P-256`, and `X9.62 prime256v1` refer to the same curve in that provider. Oracle also distinguishes legacy curves as ones that “might be more vulnerable” and “should not be used.” This is SunEC-provider documentation, not a general statement that every provider accepts those aliases or implements the same names.  
Direct source: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/security/oracle-providers.html ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/pls/topic/lookup?ctx=javase25&id=GUID-FE2D2E28-C991-4EF9-9DBE-2A4982726313))

#### Remediation documented by official sources

There is **no general Oracle/JDK remediation procedure** stating that an `ECGenParameterSpec` name outside a particular scanner allow-list must be replaced with one particular other name.

The closest documented migration/naming guidance is:

- Use the selected provider’s documented supported name(s).
- When an algorithm is standardized in a later Java Security Standard Algorithm Names specification and an earlier implementation supports it, the specification says the implementation **should use the subsequently standardized name**.  
  Direct source: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/specs/security/standard-names.html ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/specs/security/standard-names.html))
- For JDK 25 SunEC specifically, its recommended-curve table provides provider-supported preferred names and aliases; it does not provide a key, certificate, or protocol migration procedure.  
  Direct source: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/security/oracle-providers.html ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/pls/topic/lookup?ctx=javase25&id=GUID-FE2D2E28-C991-4EF9-9DBE-2A4982726313))

Accordingly, the official sources do **not** justify treating “not admitted by this CRYSL finite list” as synonymous with “not a Java-standard ECGenParameterSpec name,” “unsupported by the selected provider,” or “unsafe.”

### 3. Compatibility, formats, version support, and documented migration

#### Persisted and wire formats

The `ECGenParameterSpec` API documentation defines an in-memory parameter-spec object. It does not document:

- serialization of `ECGenParameterSpec`;
- a persisted representation of its `stdName`;
- a wire encoding for the object;
- automatic conversion of stored key material, certificates, signatures, or protocol messages when the supplied name changes.

Therefore, no API-documented persisted-format or wire-format compatibility conclusion can be made from `ECGenParameterSpec` alone.  
Direct source: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/spec/ECGenParameterSpec.html ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/spec/ECGenParameterSpec.html))

The SunEC provider documentation does document that several names/OIDs are aliases for the **same curve** within that provider—for example, the four `secp256r1` spellings listed above. That supports a provider-scoped alias-equivalence conclusion only; it does not document universal interoperability across third-party providers, serialized configuration, key encodings, certificates, or application-defined wire protocols.  
Direct source: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/security/oracle-providers.html ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/pls/topic/lookup?ctx=javase25&id=GUID-FE2D2E28-C991-4EF9-9DBE-2A4982726313))

#### Platform-version support

The class itself has existed since Java 5 (`Since: 1.5`).  
Direct source: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/spec/ECGenParameterSpec.html ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/spec/ECGenParameterSpec.html))

However, the current Java SE 25 standard-names page does **not** give per-curve “since Java version” information. It also states that providers may support additional algorithms and should document additions in release notes or provider documentation. Thus, the available evidence does not establish support for any particular name on an unspecified older JDK, newer JDK, third-party provider, FIPS provider, native provider, or hardware-backed provider.  
Direct source: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/specs/security/standard-names.html ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/specs/security/standard-names.html))

#### Migration path

Neither the `ECGenParameterSpec` Javadoc nor the Java Security Standard Algorithm Names specification documents an API-level migration path for changing the selected EC curve or its name. There is no documented automatic key conversion, key re-encoding, certificate replacement, stored-data rewrite, or protocol negotiation mechanism associated with this class.  
Direct sources:  
https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/spec/ECGenParameterSpec.html  
https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/specs/security/standard-names.html ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/spec/ECGenParameterSpec.html))

### 4. Exact matching rule in `ECGenParameterSpec.crysl`

**Source:**  
https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/ECGenParameterSpec.crysl

The source declares this governed type:

> `SPEC java.security.spec.ECGenParameterSpec`

It declares one object:

> `java.lang.String stdName;`

Its complete event/matching clause is:

> `c1: ECGenParameterSpec(stdName);`  
> `Con := c1;`

The source then requires the event:

> `ORDER`  
> `    Con`

It constrains the single constructor argument using this condition:

> `stdName in {"brainpoolP224r1", "1.3.36.3.3.2.8.1.1.5",`  
> `        "brainpoolP256r1", "1.3.36.3.3.2.8.1.1.7",`  
> `        "brainpoolP320r1", "1.3.36.3.3.2.8.1.1.9",`  
> `        "brainpoolP384r1", "1.3.36.3.3.2.8.1.1.11",`  
> `        "brainpoolP512r1", "1.3.36.3.3.2.8.1.1.13",`  
> `        "secp224r1", "NIST P-224", "1.3.132.0.33",`  
> `        "secp256r1", "NIST P-256", "X9.62 prime256v1" ,"1.2.840.10045.3.1.7",`  
> `        "secp384r1", "NIST P-384", "1.3.132.0.34",`  
> `        "secp521r1", "NIST P-521", "1.3.132.0.35"};`

The stated postcondition is:

> `preparedEC[this];`

The rule therefore matches the one-argument `ECGenParameterSpec` constructor event for the type named by its `SPEC` declaration, with one `java.lang.String` event variable named `stdName`; it then evaluates whether that variable is in the quoted finite set. The file contains **no named ordinary method events** and no events for provider selection or for other JCA types. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/ECGenParameterSpec.crysl))

**Can it match a method merely because it shares a name with the governed API?** No—not according to the source text. The rule explicitly scopes itself to:

> `SPEC java.security.spec.ECGenParameterSpec`

and its only declared event is:

> `c1: ECGenParameterSpec(stdName);`

The source contains no name-only matcher for arbitrary methods with the same spelling. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/ECGenParameterSpec.crysl))

## Source limitations and unresolved questions

- The rule file establishes only its declared type, event, order, finite membership constraint, and `preparedEC[this]` postcondition. It does not state that its list is the complete Java standard-name registry or the complete provider-supported set.
- Official JDK documentation makes provider support material. The provider, provider version, JDK version, platform, and the actual runtime `stdName` value are not provided here.
- No supplied or official source establishes whether a particular application persists this name, uses it in a protocol, or has already generated keys/certificates under it. Those questions require deployment-specific evidence and cannot be resolved from the governed API or rule text alone.
